program.checker_template:
Execute ONE saved check. Return status, evidence, confidence (0 to 1 or null), and used_dependency_ids. You receive no reference label or optimizer feedback. Do not predict what the optimizer wants.
Support checks receive source and edited images. Inspect only the saved visual proposition and binding. When dependencies are supplied, use those ancestor observations as context and investigate the more specific proposition yourself; do not simply repeat the parent answer. Use pass/fail/unknown. A pass on a broad parent does not imply a nested check passes. Known negative evidence is usable; uncertain or missing evidence is unknown. Do not award requested completion credit to supporting facts.
The requested fulfillment readout receives NO images. Use ALL and ONLY saved support observations, the original instruction, rubric and saved composition criteria. Use complete/partial/absent/unknown. Mere texture or object presence must not silently establish whole-image conversion or a requested spatial relation. Known progress plus evidenced incompleteness may be partial; absence means no requested progress. Missing necessary evidence is unknown, never a fabricated failure or completion. Do not infer new visual facts.
used_dependency_ids must name every supplied dependency check_id exactly once in saved order (empty when none). Confidence is self-report, not calibrated correctness.

actions.binding: Inspect the source and edited images. Distinguish the bowl interior from the raised lid, tank, and floor beside the toilet. Use s1 only as context and independently verify the edited image; do not treat extra frogs outside the bowl as failure or as proof of completion.

actions.criteria: For R1, complete only when the saved evidence establishes that the requested frog-in-toilet edit is fully fulfilled; a frog visibly inside the bowl establishes requested progress but does not by itself prove complete fulfillment. Partial when evidence establishes a frog added inside the bowl but does not establish complete fulfillment. Absent only when evidence shows no requested progress. Frogs on the lid, tank, or floor are not themselves requested progress and do not negate an in-bowl frog. Use all saved support observations and do not infer new visual facts.

rejected_diagnostics.semantic_rejection: The fulfillment rule is internally contradictory and cannot faithfully distinguish completion from partial fulfillment. The requested change is simply to put a frog in the toilet, and the outcome defines completion as a frog visibly within the bowl. But fulfillment says an in-bowl frog establishes progress while not by itself establishing completeness, requiring additional evidence of an unspecified condition. That adds an unsupported completion requirement and can turn a fully satisfied request into partial or unknown. The support checks also overlap: s1 and s3 both assess the same frog-in-bowl relation, while s2 repeats bowl visibility/absence assessment and is nested under s3 despite depending only on s1. This composition does not provide a distinct, justified basis for the extra completeness condition.

The support checks do not provide a reliable, non-overlapping evidence path. s1 already assesses whether a frog is inside the bowl, while s2 repeats that placement judgment despite being framed as an evidence-sufficiency check; its fail condition also conflates a visible empty bowl with sufficient evidence. s3 then asks for location evidence but its criteria say to fail when visible regions cannot be assessed, reversing the stated unknown rule and making its status ambiguous. The fulfillment readout depends on all three checks, so these defects can make completion, partial progress, or absence depend on contradictory or redundant observations rather than faithfully composed evidence.

The fulfillment composition is contradictory and can misclassify known evidence. It says complete when an inside-bowl frog is established, but also says absent when evidence establishes no frog inside, even if s3 establishes an added frog on the lid, tank, or floor. Those observations show progress toward the requested edit but not fulfillment, so the rubric requires partial—not absent. The criteria also lack a clear rule for combining s1, s3, and s2 when their observations differ or are unresolved. Revise the readout to distinguish no added frog anywhere (absent), an added frog only outside the bowl (partial), and an added frog inside the bowl (complete), while leaving insufficient or conflicting evidence unresolved.

The support checks do not provide independent, sufficient evidence for the fulfillment rule. s2 is nested under s3, but its criteria only assess bowl visibility and whether a frog is inside; it does not establish that an outside-bowl frog is an added edit relative to the source. The fulfillment rule nevertheless treats s3 as evidence of progress, so an existing frog on the lid or floor could be misclassified as requested progress. Also, s2’s fail condition (“bowl ... but no frog inside”) duplicates s1’s negative observation rather than resolving the stated evidence-sufficiency question. The composition therefore cannot reliably distinguish no progress from partial fulfillment.
